name: Gynostemma pentaphyllum (jiaogulan)

lead: Jiaogulan, or five-leaf ginseng, is a climbing vine whose leaves are brewed as a sweet tea and sold as an adaptogen. People use it hoping that better stress resilience and general health carry through to healthier-looking skin as they age.

Its leaves contain gypenosides, some chemically identical to ginseng saponins. Lab studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and small preliminary human trials have looked at blood sugar and weight. No trial has measured appearance.

paras: Most people drink it as a daily tea, though extracts and capsules are also sold. It is used as a general long-term wellness herb, often alongside other adaptogens, and results are described as gradual if noticed at all.
Wikipedia states there is no information on human toxicity, with toxicity data only from in vitro work. In the EU it is regulated as a novel food. It is sold as a supplement elsewhere.

angle.text: Jiaogulan tea and extracts are used as a ginseng-like adaptogen in longevity routines. Users link lower stress load and better general health with ageing well and healthier-looking skin; research is mostly lab-based.

lead: Gynostemma pentaphyllum, called jiaogulan or "five-leaf ginseng", is a climbing vine in the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) native to South and East Asia and New Guinea.[1] It is usually drunk as a sweet herbal tea and also sold as extracts and supplements, and is grouped with adaptogen herbs in the longevity category.[1]

For appearance, interest centres on three areas: body composition, hair and skin. Randomized trials of branded extracts have reported reductions in fat mass and abdominal fat area in overweight adults over 12 to 16 weeks [2][3], a 24-week trial reported improvements in hair elasticity, density and diameter [4], and laboratory work has reported that vesicles derived from the plant reduced UVB-induced skin-aging markers in cells and animals [5]. Trials in exercise and fatigue add a recovery angle [6][7].

Its leaves contain dammarane-type saponins, some identical to ginseng ginsenosides and others called gypenosides, plus polysaccharides, flavonoids and sterols.[1][8][9] Laboratory studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, liver-protective and cardiometabolic effects.[8][9][10][11] Wikipedia states that research is limited, that studies in cardiovascular disease, hyperlipidaemia and type 2 diabetes were too preliminary to conclude benefit, and that no information exists on human toxicity.[1]

paras: According to Wikipedia, the plant was first described in 1406 as a famine food rather than a medicine, and the herbalist Li Shizhen recorded medicinal uses in 1578 while confusing it with a similar herb.[1] The article states it has not been widely used in traditional Chinese medicine and was adopted more broadly only in recent decades.[1]

Reviews catalogue the triterpenoid saponins (gypenosides) as the main bioactive class, alongside polysaccharides and flavonoids.[8][9][12] Rodent studies report anti-inflammatory and liver-protective effects of extracts,[13][14] and a 2018 cell and animal study reported that gypenosides reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation in a diabetic cardiomyopathy model.[11] Polysaccharide fractions show antioxidant activity in vitro.[15] A review of herbal medicines for cardiovascular disease includes it among the herbs examined.[10]

A 2026 study in Bioactive Materials described extracellular vesicles derived from the plant: in UVB-exposed models they were reported to inhibit collagen degradation and DNA damage, improve skin hydration and reduce cellular senescence markers by promoting degradation of the STING protein, and the effect disappeared when STING was pharmacologically activated [5]. This is cell and animal work, not a human trial. Other reviews cover gypenosides' neuroprotective actions in animal models and the plant's anti-cancer research [16][17], and its effect on the gut microbiome as a prebiotic [18].

In T Nation threads from the mid-2000s, jiaogulan appears in a list of adaptogenic herbs that a coach said must be rotated, alongside suma, Korean ginseng and maca [19][20]. A 2009 discussion of nitric-oxide supplements lists a gypenoside-standardized Gynostemma extract among a product's ingredients [21].

Body composition: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a branded extract (ActivAMP) in 117 overweight men and women over 16 weeks, with DEXA scans, found greater reductions in body weight, BMI, total fat mass and gynoid fat mass than placebo. Visceral fat fell in men and gynoid fat in women, and plasma triglycerides, ALT and TNF-alpha differed between groups [2]. A 12-week trial of a heat-processed extract (actiponin) in 80 obese Korean adults found greater reductions than placebo in abdominal fat area, body weight, fat mass, percent body fat and BMI, with no clinically significant safety changes [3]. A registered 100-person trial of a branded product examined weight and fat loss [22].

Hair: a 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 100 adults aged 19-60 reported that the group taking the extract showed about three-fold greater gains in hair elasticity and density and four-fold in hair diameter than placebo, with better subjective satisfaction on hair damage and dryness; instrumental and visual glossiness did not differ, and no severe adverse events occurred [4].

Recovery and stress: a 12-week trial in 100 healthy Korean adults of an extract containing gypenoside L found higher VO2 max and O2 pulse, lower perceived exertion and fatigue ratings, and higher eNOS versus control [6]. A crossover trial in 16 untrained young men examined exercise performance, AMPK and mitochondrial signalling after four weeks of leaf extract [7]. An 8-week trial in 72 stressed adults found a 16.8 percent lower trait anxiety score than placebo on the STAI, while other anxiety scales did not differ significantly [23].

Lipids and metabolism: a systematic review of 22 randomized trials with 2,407 dyslipidemia participants reported effects comparable to some standard lipid agents on normalization, noting that most trials had risk-of-bias concerns [24]; a later meta-analysis of 15 studies reported lower triglycerides and higher HDL cholesterol, with mouse experiments pointing to gut-microbiota changes [25]. Registered tea trials in type 2 diabetes (16, 24 and 25 participants), a 150-person metabolic syndrome study, and a terminated Phase 2 study in acute optic neuritis (n=10) are also listed [26][27][28][29][30].

Wikipedia states that toxicity studies exist only in vitro and no information exists on human toxicity.[1] In the European Union it is treated as a novel food following a 2012 court ruling that prohibited its sale as food.[1] A survey of herbal tea products consumed in Thailand measured trace elements in the products and their infusions.[31]

lore.intro: Jiaogulan appears in training forums as an adaptogen or an ingredient inside multi-ingredient supplements rather than as a stand-alone product [19][21].
